explain.say: Spin a bicycle wheel and it keeps turning for a minute. Inside the hub, steel balls roll instead of rubbing. That is a rolling bearing. Look at the parts: the shaft turns the inner ring, the balls roll round, and the outer ring sits still in the frame.

explain.say: Rolling bearings do not wear out by rubbing; they fail by fatigue. Every pass of a ball stresses the ring surface until, after millions of passes, tiny flakes break off. Makers give a dynamic load rating C: the load at which 90 percent of bearings last one million revolutions. That is the L10 life.

explain.say: It falls eight times, to about 1400 hours! Now the other family: sliding, or journal, bearings. The shaft spins in a sleeve full of oil. Once moving, it drags oil into a thin wedge that lifts the shaft off the metal completely. See the comparison? This is hydrodynamic lubrication.

explain.say: Journal bearings are quiet and handle shocks, so car engines use them for the crankshaft. Their weak moment is starting, before the oil film forms. Superb. Exam tip: use exponent 3 for ball bearings and 10 over 3 for roller bearings in the life formula.

faq.q: What does a shaft bearing do?
faq.a: A bearing supports a turning shaft, carrying its load into the frame while letting it spin with very little friction.

faq.q: How do the balls in a bearing work?
faq.a: They roll between the inner and outer rings, so the surfaces roll rather than slide, which cuts friction. Each ball passing stresses the rings, which is why bearings eventually fail by fatigue.

faq.q: How do I calculate bearing life?
faq.a: L10 life in millions of revolutions equals C over P to the power 3 for ball bearings, or 10 over 3 for rollers. Divide by revolutions per hour to get hours.

faq.q: How does a journal bearing work?
faq.a: The shaft turns in an oil-filled sleeve. Its rotation drags oil into a converging wedge, building pressure that lifts the shaft so metal never touches metal.

faq.q: What is the difference between rolling and sliding bearings?
faq.a: Rolling bearings use balls or rollers and have low friction even at start-up. Sliding bearings ride on an oil film; they are quieter, compact and good with shocks, but need speed or pressurised oil to work well.

facts: L10 life is the life that 90 % of a group of identical bearings will reach or exceed.
Doubling the load on a ball bearing cuts its rated life by a factor of eight.
